guide.summary: Unit 5 applies marginal analysis to markets for labor, capital, and land: derived demand, marginal revenue product, marginal resource cost, hiring decisions in perfectly competitive factor markets, shifts in factor demand and supply, the least-cost and profit-maximizing combinations of inputs, and monopsony.

sections.heading: Factor demand
sections.body: Demand for a factor is derived from demand for the product it helps produce. Marginal revenue product (MRP) = MP × MR; in a perfectly competitive product market, MRP = MP × P. MRP declines as more workers are hired because of diminishing marginal returns (and, for a firm with price-setting power, falling MR). The MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labor. Factor demand shifts with changes in product demand or price, changes in productivity (technology, training), and changes in prices of other inputs (substitutes and complements).

sections.heading: Hiring in competitive labor markets
sections.body: Marginal resource (factor) cost (MRC) is the added cost of one more unit of a factor. In a perfectly competitive labor market, the firm is a wage taker: it faces a horizontal labor supply at the market wage, so MRC = wage. The firm hires until MRP = MRC. The market wage is set by market supply and demand for labor; the individual firm's supply line is drawn at that wage on side-by-side graphs. Labor supply shifts with population, preferences, education requirements, and alternative opportunities.

sections.heading: Combining inputs
sections.body: Least-cost rule: produce a given output at minimum cost by choosing inputs so MP_L/P_L = MP_K/P_K. If MP_L/w > MP_K/r, use more labor and less capital. Profit-maximizing rule: MRP_L/P_L = MRP_K/P_K = 1 (each factor's MRP equals its price).

sections.heading: Monopsony
sections.body: A monopsony is a single buyer of a factor (e.g., the only major employer in a town). It faces the upward-sloping market labor supply curve, so to hire one more worker it must raise the wage for all workers: MRC lies above the supply curve. It hires where MRP = MRC and pays the wage on the supply curve at that quantity. Compared with a competitive labor market, a monopsony hires fewer workers at a lower wage, creating deadweight loss. A minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage can increase both wages and employment.

keyTakeaways: Hire until MRP = MRC; MRC = wage in competitive labor markets.
Factor demand is derived from product demand.
Least cost: MP/P equal across inputs.
Monopsony: MRC above supply; fewer workers, lower wage.
A well-set minimum wage can raise employment under monopsony.
commonMistakes: Reading the monopsony wage from MRC instead of supply.
Using total product instead of marginal product for MRP.
Saying a perfectly competitive firm faces an upward-sloping labor supply.
Confusing the least-cost rule with the profit-maximizing rule.
Thinking a minimum wage always reduces employment.
examTips: Hiring tables: compute MP, MRP, and compare to wage row by row.
Side-by-side labor graphs: market wage set by market S and D; firm's MRC = wage horizontal.
Monopsony graphs: label MRP (D), S, MRC; mark Q_m, W_m, and the competitive point.
Input-combination questions: compute MP per dollar for each input.
guide.cramSheet:
**Derived demand:** factor demand from product demand

**MRP:** MP × P (or MP × MR) · MRP curve = labor demand

**Hire:** MRP = MRC · competitive: MRC = wage

**Shifters:** product price · productivity · other input prices

**Inputs:** least cost MP_L/w = MP_K/r · profit max MRP/P = 1

**Monopsony:** MRC above S · hire MRP = MRC · wage from S · fewer workers, lower wage

practice.stimulus:
A monopsony faces this labor supply and MRP schedule:

| Workers | Wage | MRP |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $6 | $24 |
| 2 | $8 | $20 |
| 3 | $10 | $16 |
| 4 | $12 | $12 |
| 5 | $14 | $8 |
practice.stem: How many workers does the monopsonist hire, and at what wage?
practice.explanation: Total labor cost: 6, 16, 30, 48, 70 → MRC: 6, 10, 14, 18, 22. Hire while MRP ≥ MRC: 3rd worker (16 ≥ 14), not 4th (12 < 18). Wage from supply: $10.

distractors.A: Pays MRC instead of the supply wage.

practice.stem: Using the monopsony schedule above, the government sets a minimum wage of $12. How many workers are hired?
practice.stimulus: Labor supply wages for 1–5 workers: $6, $8, $10, $12, $14. MRP for 1–5 workers: $24, $20, $16, $12, $8.
practice.explanation: With a $12 minimum, MRC = $12 for up to 4 workers (all willing at $12). Hire until MRP ≥ 12: 4 workers. Employment rises.

practice.topic: 5.2 Changes in Factor Demand and Factor Supply
practice.stem: Demand for the product made by a perfectly competitive firm increases, raising its price. In the firm's labor market (a perfectly competitive market where the firm is a wage taker), what happens?

choices.text: The wage the firm pays increases because it is a monopsony.
The firm's MRP shifts right, and it hires more workers at the market wage.

practice.explanation: MRP = MP × P rises with the product price.

practice.prompt: Millbrook Lumber is the only employer of mill workers in an isolated town and sells its lumber in a perfectly competitive product market.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a correctly labeled graph of the labor market for Millbrook, showing the MRP, labor supply, and MRC curves. Label the profit-maximizing quantity of workers Q_m and wage W_m.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: On your graph, label the quantity Q_c and wage W_c that would occur if the labor market were perfectly competitive.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The government sets a minimum wage equal to W_c. Will employment at Millbrook increase, decrease, or stay the same? Explain.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: If the price of lumber rises, what happens to Millbrook's demand for workers? Explain.

rubric.description: Axes wage and quantity of labor; downward-sloping MRP (D); upward-sloping S; MRC above S.
Q_m where MRP = MRC; W_m on the supply curve at Q_m (below MRP).
Q_c and W_c at the intersection of MRP and S; Q_c > Q_m and W_c > W_m.
Increase: the minimum wage makes MRC horizontal at W_c up to the supply curve, so the firm hires until MRP = W_c, at Q_c.
Increases: MRP = MP × P rises, shifting labor demand right.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) The graph has 'Wage' on the vertical axis and 'Quantity of workers' on the horizontal axis. MRP = D slopes downward, labor supply S slopes upward, and MRC slopes upward more steeply, lying above S. Millbrook hires Q_m where MRP = MRC and pays wage W_m, found by going down from that intersection to the supply curve.

(b) The competitive outcome is where MRP intersects S, at Q_c and W_c, with Q_c greater than Q_m and W_c greater than W_m.

(c) Employment increases. With a minimum wage at W_c, Millbrook can hire any number of workers up to Q_c at the same wage, so its MRC is constant at W_c. It hires until MRP = W_c, which occurs at Q_c, more than Q_m.

(d) Millbrook's demand for workers increases. A higher lumber price raises each worker's marginal revenue product (MP × P), shifting the MRP curve to the right.
